atlas-dk.0127: Graduate programmes are salaried, full-time, fixed-term jobs of typically 18 to 24 months with rotation between departments; a standard working week is 37 hours.
atlas-dk.0128: Probation, notice periods and any extra month of pay are set by the contract and the collective agreement; read them before signing.
atlas-dk.0129: Under the Fast-track scheme the employer must be certified by SIRI, the job must pay at least DKK 552,000 a year on the Pay Limit track or DKK 446,000 on the Supplementary track, and the employer applies online with your power of attorney. Ask a prospective employer whether it is certified.
atlas-dk.0130: The Pay Limit scheme needs no specific education or field, only an offer of at least DKK 552,000 a year; processing normally takes about a month and up to three if more information is needed, so raise the permit at the offer stage.
atlas-dk.0131: The Supplementary Pay Limit track needs the job posted on Jobnet and EURES for at least two weeks, so the employer runs a short advertisement before it can hire you on that track.
atlas-dk.0132: Novo Nordisk’s International Operations tracks employ you in a named hiring country and its global tracks are employed by the headquarters, and it asks for full international mobility; the page does not mention permits.
atlas-dk.0133: Posted vacancies: Workindenmark’s Jobnet portal, Jobindex (with an English version) and the employers’ own career pages. Jobindex showed about 36,500 jobs when read.
atlas-dk.0134: Graduate programmes: Jobbank.dk lists 107 with duration, application months and start, and Workindenmark’s graduate page explains the format. Danske Bank directs applicants to its own careers site.
atlas-dk.0135: English-language jobs: jobsinenglish.dk scans Danish employers’ ads; in 2024 DTU (244), Grundfos (112), MAN Energy Solutions (92), Terma (60) and Topsoe (55) advertised the most English-only jobs, though it misses Novo Nordisk, Maersk and Lego.
atlas-dk.0136: University and fairs: Copenhagen Business School’s graduate event, Danske Bank’s career events and Workindenmark’s job-fair calendar; to be found by recruiters abroad, export a Europass CV to the EURES portal.
atlas-dk.0137: Missing the programme window: the main intakes close between December and April, and Novo Nordisk’s postings were visible only from 14 November to 5 December 2025.
atlas-dk.0138: Sending a generic or long cover letter: it should be a single A4 page, written for the position, and say why this job and this company.
atlas-dk.0139: Asking a stranger for a job in the first message: the advice is to ask for advice first, and to phone before an unsolicited application.
atlas-dk.0140: Putting sensitive personal data on the CV, such as the CPR or passport number, or treating Danske Bank as having a classic graduate programme; its careers page names none.
atlas-dk.0141: Arriving at an interview too early, or with technical problems for an online one: both count against you.
atlas-dk.0142: Nordea’s graduate programme asks for excellent English and names no Danish requirement; no certificate is named, the online test and interviews are the evidence.
atlas-dk.0143: Novo Nordisk’s corporate language is English and it asks for fluent written and spoken English; some International Operations tracks add local-language requirements, and mid-sized Danish firms often want Danish at junior and middle levels.
atlas-dk.0144: Many engineering and technology employers advertise English-only jobs (DTU, Grundfos, MAN Energy Solutions, Terma, Topsoe), and the retail groups Salling, Bestseller and JYSK also appear among the top 20, probably for IT.
atlas-dk.0145: The public programmes on Jobbank.dk do not state a language requirement; Workindenmark says some jobs need Danish, and public bodies work in Danish, so expect to need it.
atlas-dk.0146: The 53% of international master’s graduates working in Denmark two years out is an average dominated by technical and health fields; business graduates are below it (CBS 46%), and the Danish graduates themselves spent on average 23.3% of their first twelve months unemployed.
atlas-dk.0147: No source read gives a return-offer or conversion rate for Danish student jobs or programmes, and none gives time to first job for internationals.
atlas-dk.0148: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens need no visa or work permit. Within three months (six if looking for work), apply online (form OD1) for the EU residence document; it is free.
atlas-dk.0149: Then register an address to get your CPR number and the yellow health card, which gives free public health care; book at International Citizen Service (ICS).
atlas-dk.0150: Salaries go to a Danish account registered as your NemKonto.
atlas-dk.0152: The university starts form ST1 online and you complete it, then give biometrics at a consulate or VFS centre. Non-EU students pay tuition.
atlas-dk.0153: Work up to 90 hours a month from September to May and full time in June, July and August; self-employment is not allowed.
atlas-dk.0154: Denmark is outside the EU rules on student mobility: a student permit from another EU country gives no right to study here, Erasmus included.
atlas-dk.0155: DKK 7,426 a month (DKK 89,112 a year), in your own account
atlas-dk.0156: Working even one hour over 90 a month in term is illegal work and can cost the permit.
atlas-dk.0158: For people aged 18 to 35 whose internship is part of a degree abroad, or within 12 months of graduating; an internship agreement, collective-agreement pay and accident insurance, for up to 18 months, only with that host.
atlas-dk.0159: Students already in Denmark do an internship their degree requires on their student permit.
atlas-dk.0162: Job-search stay after a Danish degree
atlas-dk.0163: After a Danish degree you can stay to look for work: three years if your study application was filed before 1 October 2026, one year if filed later; PhD graduates keep three years.
atlas-dk.0164: During the search you keep student work rights (90 hours a month); a job at the pay-limit levels lets you start work on the day you apply for the work permit.
atlas-dk.0165: The old establishment card was abolished on 1 April 2023; offers built on it are out of date.
atlas-dk.0167: The pay limit scheme needs only a salary above the threshold, paid into a Danish account; the supplementary scheme a lower salary and a job advertised for two weeks on Jobnet and EURES. Neither needs a specific degree.
atlas-dk.0168: With a certified employer (fast track) you may start work as soon as the application and biometrics are in, without waiting for the decision. Jobs on the positive lists need a degree or skilled qualification in that occupation.
atlas-dk.0173: Benefits such as a car, housing or uncertain bonuses do not count towards the pay limit.
atlas-dk.0175: Below those levels the job must be advertised on Jobnet and EURES for two weeks with no suitable Danish or EU candidate, the regional labour council is consulted, and pay must follow Danish collective agreements.
atlas-dk.0177: A Danish PhD is a salaried job under the academics’ collective agreement, with 17.1% pension paid by the employer; the university starts form PHD1.
atlas-dk.0178: A guest researcher invited but not paid by a Danish institution applies on form AR1 and must show their own means.
atlas-dk.0182: Denmark has working-holiday agreements only with Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Chile and Argentina.
atlas-dk.0183: For citizens of the partner countries aged 18 to 30 (35 for Australia and Canada): 12 months, work for at most six (nine for Canadians) and no more than three with one employer.
atlas-dk.0184: Up to 90 days in any 180; no ordinary paid work, only meetings or unpaid guest lectures. Other nationalities may need a Schengen visa.
atlas-dk.0185: Book your appointment online at icitizen.dk at one of the International Citizen Service centres (Copenhagen, Aarhus, Odense, Aalborg), which handle residence, civil registration, health card and tax in one visit.
atlas-dk.0186: Give your biometrics (photo and fingerprints) at a Danish mission or visa centre abroad, or at SIRI on arrival, as part of the permit application.
atlas-dk.0187: Register in the civil register (Folkeregister) with a valid lease (lejekontrakt) or a written statement from the landlord: that is what gives you a CPR number.
atlas-dk.0188: Show your work contract or university enrolment letter to receive the EU registration certificate (registreringsbevis).
atlas-dk.0189: Confirm your presence at SIRI or the centre, and the residence card (opholdskort) arrives by post within 2 to 4 weeks.
atlas-dk.0190: The 10-digit CPR number (birth date plus four digits) is the key to banking, leases, phone contracts, health care and pay.
atlas-dk.0191: With it, fill in your income estimate (forskudsopgørelse) at skat.dk to get a tax card: without one, your employer must withhold 55% tax, plus the 8% labour market contribution.
atlas-dk.0192: Registering gives you the yellow health card (sundhedskort), with your CPR number and assigned GP: it makes GP and hospital care free.
atlas-dk.0193: Activate MitID, the national digital ID used for borger.dk, skat.dk, the state digital post and online banking: in the app by scanning your passport chip, or in person at Borgerservice.
atlas-dk.0194: Open an account at a Danish bank and register it as your NemKonto: employers and every public body pay into it through your CPR number.
atlas-dk.0195: Apply to extend or change status before your permit expires to keep the right to stay while you wait.
